- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.4), model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive sell-off bias.  
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., > +1.5% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to correct; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive (e.g., 0.0 to +0.3), model frequently overestimates upward momentum; cap forecast growth at 0.5–0.8% above prior day.  
- Mean reversion is strong in 30-day horizon; if forecast is > 1.5σ above recent 10-day average, reduce by 0.3–0.5σ to align with historical volatility.  
- When sentiment is positive but weak (e.g., +0.1 to +0.2), model often underestimates upside; add 0.1–0.3 to forecast for early momentum.  
- Lagged sentiment (e.g., 3–5 day sentiment) often predicts 1–2 day price shift; use 3-day sentiment as a proxy for 1-day forecast adjustment.  
- Avoid forecasting > 2.0σ above or below 30-day moving average unless sentiment is extreme; use sentiment as a volatility filter to cap extremes.
